about: How Bhojpuri is typed in Latin letters: native word -> canonical romanisation (the first spelling of every slot), weighted chat spellings, and the skeleton folds the romanised lookup keys on. Read by training/mlkb/langs/romanisation.py; the weights are fitted to Aksharantar hin, Hindi's pairs, as there are none for Bhojpuri (training/mlkb/langs/calibrate.py). Each table maps a letter (or a letter + nukta, or a conjunct) to [spelling, weight] options, canonical first.

skeleton.about: Applied to typed Latin and to the canonical romanisation alike: lowercase a-z only; the longest `replace` key at each position (else `letters`, else the letter itself); a symbol equal to the one before it is dropped (doubled letters); every `dropBetweenConsonants` letter with a consonant on both sides is dropped; then a final vowel in `dropFinal` after a consonant is dropped.

looseSpelling.about: Which typed spellings spell a word out, for ranking (the engine's Romanisation::relaxed). Vowel length only, as for Hindi: Bhojpuri keeps d and t apart (द, त), so no letter is read as another.

notes.inherent: The inherent vowel is typed 'a' inside a word and dropped at its end (घर ghar). Speech drops it inside words too (करत karat, करतानी kartani), and typists follow speech or the letters; the skeleton drops every a between two consonants so both give one key.
notes.letters: ऽ (avagraha) lengthens the vowel before it and is typed as nothing or as a (कऽ ka, हऽ ha); it is a final in the tables. Candrabindu is n or nothing (हँ han / ha, में men / me), anusvara n, or m before a labial. ज्ञ is gy (ज्ञान gyan). A nukta letter is its consonant plus U+093C after NFC, so its key is two code points; ड़ is r or d (बड़ bar / bad, लइका and लड़िका).
notes.skeleton: Aspirates fold to their plain letters, sh and chh/ch to s and c, z to j, f to p, w to v, q to k; aa, ee and oo to a, i and u; mb and mp to nb and np. A final a after a consonant is dropped, which covers the final inherent vowel typed or not.
notes.unwritten: A final candrabindu or anusvara after a vowel is as often left unwritten (में me, नाहीं nahi, काहें kahe), so optionalFinals names both: such a word is also keyed by the skeleton of its walk without the n, and either spelling spells it out; a final न is always written. The dropped medial vowel is often written u (hum for हम, humar for हमार), so alsoBetweenConsonants u: typed letters with a u between consonants are also looked up with it dropped, behind the words that have the u. On the held-out rows (Hindi words, whose annotators wrote every final nasal) the two together move the first native suggestion from 39.9% to 39.7% and leave the bar at 42.0%.
